sectionGuide.why: Realised reliability improves through design patterns (verification loops, proactive grounding) and corrections (retry, HITL, rollback) — not only by selecting a better model. The charter explicitly covers correction mechanisms and human-intervention boundaries.
sectionGuide.wgUse: Reliability-by-design patterns and operational runbooks. Specifies when human-in-the-loop vs automation is required. Closes the failure → remediation loop. Review after failure P0 and governance P0 are settled.
sectionGuide.enables: Closes the loop from failures to remediation; evaluation protocols can specify when automation vs HITL is required; connects to governance (recoverability, escalation).
sectionGuide.priorities: **P0** (self-correction) is the foundational correction concept — may appear in the P1 JSON file when it is the sole P0 term. **P1** = reliability-by-design patterns and primary correction mechanisms. **P2** = operational controls (circuit breakers, policy gates).

categories.relevance: Charter scope: react when failures occur — retry, HITL, rollback, escalation — human-intervention boundaries.
categories.wgUse: Operational runbooks · protocol branches · solution landscape comparisons

categories.relevance: Charter scope: prevent failures before they happen (verification loops, proactive grounding, policy gates).
categories.wgUse: Reliability-by-design guidance · automation vs HITL requirements · closes loop from failure patterns

terms.definition: An automated pattern that detects a likely error in a draft output or trajectory and attempts revision — for example re-querying a source, re-running validation, or replanning — before finalising.
terms.scopeNote: Reactive correction. Failure of this pattern is recovery failure. Distinct from proactive verification loops.
terms.literatureNote: Reactive recovery patterns. SRE names (circuit breaker, rollback) linked in academicTerms where relevant.

terms.definition: A defined response applied after a failure is detected or suspected — such as retry, rollback, fallback, escalation, or human review. Charter classifies what can be automated vs what requires human intervention.
terms.scopeNote: Distinct from reliability-by-design patterns that prevent failure upstream.
terms.literatureNote: Reactive recovery patterns. SRE names (circuit breaker, rollback) linked in academicTerms where relevant.

terms.definition: Handing a task, decision, or exception to a higher authority — another agent tier, an orchestrator rule, or a human operator — when automated recovery is exhausted or policy requires it.
terms.scopeNote: Signalling deliverables define handoff formats and triggers.
terms.literatureNote: Reactive recovery patterns. SRE names (circuit breaker, rollback) linked in academicTerms where relevant.

terms.definition: A checkpoint where a human must approve, edit, or reject an agent action or output before the system may proceed. Used when stakes, ambiguity, or policy require human judgment.
terms.scopeNote: Charter: human intervention category and escalation trigger. Also a reliability-by-design pattern when placed before sensitive actions.
terms.literatureNote: Accepted in HITL and enterprise AI literature. AAIF scopes when human intervention is a correction mechanism vs part of the workflow object.

terms.definition: Re-attempting a failed step — such as a tool call, model generation, or sub-task — within a bounded budget and backoff policy.
terms.scopeNote: Can improve operational fault robustness or cause recovery failure if unbounded.
terms.literatureNote: Reactive recovery patterns. SRE names (circuit breaker, rollback) linked in academicTerms where relevant.

terms.definition: Designing the agent to assemble context from authorised sources, structured tool results, and trust anchors by default — rather than relying on uncited model knowledge for high-stakes facts.
terms.scopeNote: Implements charter grounding to authoritative data sources.
terms.literatureNote: Proactive patterns that improve realised reliability. Less standardised in benchmarks than failure or accuracy terms.

terms.definition: Architectural choices made before runtime to improve accuracy and reliability — such as grounding to authoritative sources, verification before action, bounded delegation, and validated specifications — rather than relying on retries after failure.
terms.scopeNote: Charter guiding principle. reliability-by-design guidance translates patterns from this taxonomy.
terms.literatureNote: Proactive patterns that improve realised reliability. Less standardised in benchmarks than failure or accuracy terms.

terms.definition: A deliberate step that validates evidence, policy, or output structure before the agent commits an answer or action — using deterministic checks, secondary review, or trust anchors where stakes are high.
terms.scopeNote: Proactive pattern. Distinct from reactive self-correction after a failure is already suspected.
terms.literatureNote: Proactive patterns that improve realised reliability. Less standardised in benchmarks than failure or accuracy terms.
